newsitem.title: USA: Russian spacecraft returns to Earth over S.Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Russian spacecraft returns to Earth over S.Pacific.

text.p: Russia's crippled Mars probe, carrying four canisters of radioactive plutonium, fell to Earth on Sunday over the South Pacific west of Chile, U.S. and Australian officials said.

U.S. Space Command in Colorado Springs, Co., which had been monitoring the stricken spacecraft's orbit, said it reentered Earth's atmosphere above "a broad ocean area somewhere west of Chile" at about 8:30 p.m. EST (0130 GMT).
Australian officials said the probe landed between Easter Island and the Chilean coast and located the impact site at 31 degrees South, 96.3 degrees West.

U.S. Space command spokesman Dave Knox said his agency tracked objects in space, not in the atmosphere, therefore it was impossible to know at this point whether the six-tonne spacecraft exploded upon reentry, and where exactly the resulting debris landed.
"We have confirmed that the spacecraft has reentered. There's no way for us to tell if something survived reentry," Knox told Reuters.
If the Russian probe survived reentry, it may have crashed into the Southern Pacific several hundred miles from the calculated reentry location.
Most of the spacecraft's weight was in fuel, which would likely have burned up or exploded upon entering the Earth's atmosphere, Knox said.

The status of the four small batteries containing 200 grams of plutonium was unclear. Aircraft with sensoring equipment were expected to scan the reentry area for signs of radioactivity, U.S. officials said.

The White House earlier said that the probe, which ran into trouble after blasting off from Kazakhstan on Saturday, could hit Earth over Australia, causing Australian defence officials to prepare for a possible emergency.

"There is no danger to anyone and that is very good news," U.S. National Security Council official Robert Bell told CNN just moments before the spacecraft came back to Earth, and after it was clear it would not strike Australia after all.
The spacecraft lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday, but failed to break out of the Earth's orbit after a booster rocket misfired.
Bell told reporters in a telephone conference call the craft was expected to burn up on reentry, but two landing vehicles were expected to survive.

NASA officials said the vehicles were built to survive a landing on Mars and weighed 110 pounds (50 kilos) each. Two 6.5-foot (2-metre) penetrators designed to ram into the surface of Mars and weighing 143 pounds (65 kilos) each, were also expected to survive reentry into the Earth's atmosphere.
The landing vehicles each carried two tiny plutonium batteries about the size of 35mm film canisters containing a total of 200 grams of the radioactive material.

"The Russian space agency has informed NASA that these batteries are designed to withstand great heat and great stress on impact," Bell said. He said Russian assessments that there was little danger of radioactive contamination of the environment was "very reassuring."
The Russian probe had been due to reach Mars on Sept. 12 next year. The failed mission was the second of three planned trips from Earth to Mars in just over a month.

The United States launched a robot voyage to Mars two weeks ago and a second mission will blast off on Dec. 2. All were tasked to check for signs of water on the far-away planet -- a key clue to whether there was once life on Mars.
Bell said a misfiring of a fourth stage of the probe's booster rocket had doomed the Russian Mars probe.

Bell, a special assistant to President Bill Clinton and a senior director of the NSC for defence policy, said there were "a couple of scenarios that could be a worst case," but stressed all were "extremely unlikely."
One was that the plutonium canisters would break up. If this happened at high altitude, Bell said a small radioactive cloud that would result would dissipate harmlessly.

"If some cloud of dispersal were formed at a lower altitude and inhaled by humans, it could be lethal," Bell said. He said there could also be a localised danger if the canisters broke up upon impact.

The Russian space mishap was the fourth incident of its kind in recent years. A U.S. space vehicle, Skylab, plunged to Earth over Western Australia in 1979 without causing damage and a Russian Cosmos satellite fell in an unhabited region of Canada in 1987.
In 1991 the Soviet space station Salyut 7 reentered the Earth's atmosphere and the debris was believed to have landed in the Atlantic Oceon, though some pieces were reportedly found in Argentina.
